title: Life Processes
description: Grade 10 Biology: nutrition (autotrophic & heterotrophic, human digestion), respiration, transportation in humans and plants, and excretion — notes, examples and a test.

topics.title: What Are Life Processes? Autotrophic Nutrition
topics.concept:
The basic functions that an organism must carry out to maintain and sustain life are called life processes. They include nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion (along with control & coordination and reproduction). These processes keep the body working, repair worn-out parts and provide energy — even when the organism appears to be at rest.

Nutrition is the process of taking in food and using it for energy, growth and repair. Based on how they obtain food, organisms show two main modes:

  • Autotrophic nutrition — the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances. Green plants and some bacteria are autotrophs.
  • Heterotrophic nutrition — the organism depends on others for food. Animals and fungi are heterotrophs.

Green plants make food by photosynthesis: using carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of sunlight and the green pigment chlorophyll, they produce glucose and release oxygen.

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll)

The main events are: (1) absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, (2) conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen, and (3) reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrate. Gases enter and leave the leaf through tiny pores called stomata, whose opening and closing is controlled by guard cells. The glucose made is often stored as starch.

examples.problem: Example 1: List the raw materials a green plant needs for photosynthesis, and name the products.
examples.solution:
Recall the photosynthesis equation.

  • Raw materials: carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll.
  • Products: glucose (food) and oxygen.
examples.answer: Raw materials: CO2, water, sunlight and chlorophyll. Products: glucose and oxygen.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the role of stomata and guard cells in a leaf?
examples.solution:
Stomata are pores for gas exchange.

  • Stomata allow exchange of gases (CO2 in, O2 out) and loss of water vapour.
  • Guard cells around each stoma control its opening and closing.
examples.answer: Stomata are tiny pores for gas exchange and water vapour loss; guard cells open and close them.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is sunlight essential for autotrophic nutrition?
examples.solution:
Photosynthesis is powered by light.

  • Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
  • This energy is used to convert CO2 and water into glucose; without it, food cannot be made.
examples.answer: Because chlorophyll absorbs sunlight and its energy drives the making of glucose from CO2 and water; without light no food is made.

recap:
• Life processes (nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion) maintain life.
  • Autotrophs make their own food; heterotrophs depend on others.
  • Photosynthesis: CO2 + water → glucose + O2, using sunlight and chlorophyll.
  • Gas exchange occurs through stomata controlled by guard cells; glucose is stored as starch.

quiz.q: The green pigment that traps sunlight for photosynthesis is:
quiz.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: The tiny pores in a leaf through which gases are exchanged are:
quiz.explanation: Stomata are the leaf pores for gas exchange, controlled by guard cells.

topics.title: Heterotrophic Nutrition and Nutrition in Humans
topics.concept:
In heterotrophic nutrition organisms take in food made by others. It is of three main types: saprotrophic (feeding on dead, decaying matter, e.g. fungi), parasitic (feeding on a living host, e.g. Cuscuta, ticks) and holozoic (taking in whole food and digesting it inside the body, e.g. humans, Amoeba).

In humans, nutrition is holozoic and takes place in the alimentary canal (digestive tract) with the help of associated glands. The journey of food:

  • Mouth — teeth chew the food; saliva (from salivary glands) contains the enzyme salivary amylase that begins digesting starch into sugar.
  • Oesophagus (food pipe) — pushes food to the stomach by wave-like muscular movements called peristalsis.
  • Stomach — gastric glands release hydrochloric acid (kills germs, makes the medium acidic), the enzyme pepsin (digests proteins) and mucus (protects the stomach lining).
  • Small intestine — the main site of digestion and absorption. It receives bile from the liver (emulsifies fats) and pancreatic juice from the pancreas (trypsin for proteins, lipase for fats, amylase for starch). Its own juice completes digestion. The inner wall has finger-like villi that greatly increase surface area for absorption of digested food into the blood.
  • Large intestine — absorbs water; the undigested waste (faeces) is removed through the anus (egestion).

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three types of heterotrophic nutrition and give an example of each.
examples.solution:
Heterotrophs differ in how they obtain food.

  • Saprotrophic — fungi (on dead matter).
  • Parasitic — Cuscuta or ticks (on a living host).
  • Holozoic — humans, Amoeba (whole food taken in).

examples.problem: Example 2: State the role of (a) hydrochloric acid and (b) bile in digestion.
examples.solution:
Recall the action in stomach and small intestine.

  • (a) HCl kills germs and makes the medium acidic for pepsin to act.
  • (b) Bile emulsifies fats (breaks them into small droplets) and makes the medium alkaline.
examples.answer: (a) HCl kills germs and provides an acidic medium for pepsin; (b) bile emulsifies fats and makes the medium alkaline.

examples.problem: Example 3: How are villi suited to their function in the small intestine?
examples.solution:
Villi are adapted for absorption.

  • They are tiny finger-like projections that greatly increase the surface area.
  • They have a rich blood supply, so digested food is absorbed efficiently into the blood.
examples.answer: Villi are finger-like projections with a rich blood supply that increase surface area for efficient absorption of digested food.

recap:
• Heterotrophic nutrition: saprotrophic, parasitic, holozoic.
  • Human digestion: mouth (salivary amylase → starch), stomach (HCl + pepsin → proteins), small intestine (bile, pancreatic juice; main digestion & absorption via villi), large intestine (absorbs water).
  • Peristalsis moves food along the gut.
  • Undigested waste is egested through the anus.

quiz.q: The enzyme in saliva that begins the digestion of starch is:
quiz.explanation: Salivary amylase in the mouth starts breaking down starch into sugar.

quiz.q: Most digestion and absorption of food occurs in the:
quiz.explanation: The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption (via villi).

topics.title: Respiration
topics.concept:
Respiration is the process of breaking down food (glucose) to release energy for the body’s use. The energy is stored in molecules of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the ‘energy currency’ of the cell. Respiration is of two types:

  • Aerobic respiration — takes place in the presence of oxygen, in the mitochondria. Glucose is completely broken down into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy.
  • Anaerobic respiration — takes place without oxygen. In yeast, glucose → ethanol + CO2 (fermentation); in our muscle cells during heavy exercise, glucose → lactic acid, releasing less energy. The build-up of lactic acid causes muscle cramps.

In humans, air is taken in through the respiratory system: nostrils → nasal cavity → trachea (windpipe, kept open by rings of cartilage) → two bronchi → bronchioles → tiny air sacs called alveoli in the lungs. The alveoli have thin walls and a rich network of blood capillaries, where exchange of gases occurs: oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out to be breathed out. Oxygen is carried in the blood by the red pigment haemoglobin in red blood cells.

In plants, gas exchange occurs through stomata (leaves), lenticels (stems) and the root surface; there is no special transport of gases as in animals.

examples.problem: Example 1: Compare the products and energy released in aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.
examples.solution:
Compare the two pathways.

  • Aerobic (with O2): glucose → CO2 + water, releasing much energy.
  • Anaerobic (without O2, in muscles): glucose → lactic acid, releasing less energy.
examples.answer: Aerobic: CO2 + water with much energy. Anaerobic (muscles): lactic acid with less energy.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why do our muscles sometimes cramp during heavy exercise?
examples.solution:
Heavy exercise can outrun the oxygen supply.

  • When oxygen runs short, muscles respire anaerobically.
  • This produces lactic acid, whose build-up causes cramps.
examples.answer: Because muscles respire anaerobically when oxygen is short, producing lactic acid whose build-up causes cramps.

examples.problem: Example 3: How are alveoli well suited for the exchange of gases?
examples.solution:
Alveoli are adapted for diffusion.

  • They have very thin walls and a large total surface area.
  • They are surrounded by many blood capillaries, so gases diffuse rapidly.
examples.answer: Alveoli have thin walls, a large surface area and a rich blood supply, allowing rapid exchange of gases.

recap:
• Respiration releases energy from glucose, stored as ATP.
  • Aerobic (in mitochondria, with O2) → CO2 + water + much energy; anaerobic (no O2) → ethanol (yeast) or lactic acid (muscles) + less energy.
  • Human path: nostrils → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (gas exchange).
  • Haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.

quiz.q: Aerobic respiration in the cell takes place in the:
quiz.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration (the 'powerhouse' of the cell).

quiz.q: Anaerobic respiration in human muscles produces:
quiz.explanation: In muscles without enough oxygen, glucose breaks down into lactic acid.

topics.title: Transportation in Humans and Plants
topics.concept:
Transportation carries materials (food, oxygen, carbon dioxide, wastes) to and from cells. In humans, this is done by the circulatory system — the heart, blood and blood vessels.

  • The heart has four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles. The right side handles deoxygenated blood (to the lungs) and the left side handles oxygenated blood (to the body). Because blood passes through the heart twice in one full cycle, it is called double circulation, and the oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix — this is efficient for warm-blooded animals.
  • Blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick walls, high pressure); veins carry blood back to the heart (have valves to prevent back-flow); capillaries are very thin vessels where exchange of materials with cells occurs.
  • Blood contains plasma, red blood cells (carry O2 via haemoglobin), white blood cells (fight disease) and platelets (help clotting). Lymph is another fluid that helps transport and immunity.

In plants there are two transport tissues: xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots to the leaves; the pull is created mainly by transpiration (loss of water vapour from leaves). Phloem carries food (made in leaves) to all parts of the plant; this movement is called translocation and requires energy.

examples.problem: Example 1: Differentiate between arteries and veins (two points).
examples.solution:
Compare direction and structure.

  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart, have thick walls and no valves.
  • Veins carry blood towards the heart, have thinner walls and valves to prevent back-flow.
examples.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick walls, no valves); veins carry blood to the heart (thinner walls, with valves).

examples.problem: Example 2: What is double circulation and why is it advantageous?
examples.solution:
Blood passes through the heart twice per cycle.

  • Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate.
  • This ensures an efficient oxygen supply, useful for warm-blooded animals with high energy needs.
examples.answer: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice per cycle, keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate for efficient oxygen supply.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the plant tissues that transport (a) water and minerals and (b) food.
examples.solution:
Recall the two conducting tissues.

  • (a) Xylem transports water and minerals upward.
  • (b) Phloem transports food (translocation).
examples.answer: (a) Xylem carries water and minerals; (b) phloem carries food.

recap:
• Human transport = heart (4 chambers), blood and vessels; double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.
  • Arteries carry blood away (thick walls); veins carry it back (valves); capillaries allow exchange.
  • Plant xylem carries water/minerals up (driven by transpiration); phloem carries food (translocation).

quiz.q: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are:
quiz.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, usually at high pressure.

quiz.q: In plants, water and minerals are transported by the:
quiz.explanation: Xylem carries water and minerals upward; phloem carries food.

topics.title: Excretion in Humans and Plants
topics.concept:
Excretion is the removal of harmful nitrogenous and other metabolic wastes from the body. In humans, the excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, two ureters, a urinary bladder and the urethra.

  • The kidneys filter waste (mainly urea) from the blood and produce urine.
  • The basic filtering unit of the kidney is the nephron. Each kidney has about a million nephrons. In a nephron, blood is filtered in a cup-shaped structure (Bowman’s capsule around a ball of capillaries, the glomerulus); then, as the filtrate passes along the tubule, useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and most water are reabsorbed back into the blood. The remaining liquid is urine.
  • Urine passes through the ureters to the urinary bladder, where it is stored, and is removed through the urethra.

When the kidneys fail, wastes build up in the blood. They can be removed by an artificial process called dialysis using a dialysis machine (artificial kidney).

In plants, excretion is simpler. Plants get rid of excess water by transpiration; oxygen and carbon dioxide are released through stomata; and many waste products are stored in leaves that fall off, in bark, or as gums, resins and latex. Some wastes are also released into the surrounding soil.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the basic filtering unit of the kidney and the main nitrogenous waste removed in urine.
examples.solution:
Recall kidney structure and waste.

  • The filtering unit is the nephron.
  • The main nitrogenous waste removed is urea.
examples.answer: The filtering unit is the nephron; the main nitrogenous waste is urea.

examples.problem: Example 2: During urine formation, which useful substances are reabsorbed back into the blood?
examples.solution:
Selective reabsorption saves useful materials.

  • Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed.
  • Most of the water and useful salts are also reabsorbed.
examples.answer: Glucose, amino acids, useful salts and most of the water are reabsorbed into the blood.

examples.problem: Example 3: State any two ways in which plants get rid of their waste products.
examples.solution:
Plants store or release wastes in several ways.

  • Excess water is lost by transpiration; gases leave through stomata.
  • Wastes are stored in leaves/bark that fall off, or as gums, resins and latex.
examples.answer: Plants lose excess water by transpiration and release gases through stomata; they also store wastes in falling leaves/bark or as gums, resins and latex.

recap:
• Excretion removes nitrogenous wastes (mainly urea).
  • Human system: kidneys (filtering unit = nephron) → ureters → bladder → urethra.
  • Useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, water) are reabsorbed; dialysis helps when kidneys fail.
  • Plants excrete via transpiration, stomata, falling leaves/bark, and gums/resins/latex.

quiz.q: The basic filtering unit of the kidney is the:
quiz.explanation: The nephron is the kidney's basic filtration unit.

quiz.q: When kidneys fail, blood is cleaned of wastes by the artificial process of:
quiz.explanation: Dialysis removes wastes from the blood when the kidneys cannot.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a life process?
questions.explanation: Rusting is a chemical change in metals, not a life process.

questions.q: Organisms that prepare their own food are called:
questions.explanation: Autotrophs, like green plants, make their own food.

questions.q: The raw materials for photosynthesis are:
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water (with sunlight and chlorophyll).

questions.q: Gaseous exchange in a leaf takes place through the:
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores for gas exchange, controlled by guard cells.

questions.q: Salivary amylase begins the digestion of:
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into sugar in the mouth.

questions.q: The enzyme pepsin, which digests proteins, acts in the:
questions.explanation: Pepsin acts in the acidic medium of the stomach to digest proteins.

questions.q: Bile, which helps digest fats by emulsification, is produced by the:
questions.explanation: Bile is produced by the liver and emulsifies fats.

questions.q: The finger-like projections that increase surface area for absorption in the small intestine are:
questions.explanation: Villi increase the surface area for absorption of digested food.

questions.q: Aerobic respiration takes place in the:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces ethanol and:
questions.explanation: In yeast, glucose breaks down into ethanol and carbon dioxide (fermentation).

questions.q: Exchange of gases in the lungs occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The thin-walled alveoli are the site of gas exchange.

questions.q: The human heart has how many chambers?
questions.explanation: The human heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.

questions.q: In plants, food prepared in the leaves is transported by the:
questions.explanation: Phloem transports food (translocation); xylem carries water and minerals.

questions.q: The basic filtering unit of the kidney is the:
questions.explanation: The nephron is the kidney's filtering unit.

questions.q: The main nitrogenous waste excreted in human urine is:
questions.explanation: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste removed by the kidneys.

questions.q: A potted plant is kept in the dark for 48 hours and then a leaf is tested with iodine. It does not turn blue-black because:
options: No starch was made without light (photosynthesis stopped)
Iodine does not work in the dark
questions.explanation: Without light, photosynthesis stops, so no starch forms and iodine gives no blue-black colour.

questions.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?
options: It pumps blood to the whole body, against greater resistance
It pumps blood only to the lungs
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body, needing more force, so its wall is thicker.

questions.q: An athlete breathes faster and deeper during a race mainly to:
options: Supply more oxygen for aerobic respiration in muscles
questions.explanation: Hard exercise needs more oxygen for aerobic respiration to release energy, so breathing rate increases.

questions.q: Reabsorption of glucose and most water in the nephron ensures that:
options: Useful substances are not lost in urine
questions.explanation: Selective reabsorption returns useful glucose, salts and water to the blood, so only waste is excreted.

questions.q: Transpiration is useful to a plant because, besides cooling it, it mainly helps to:
options: Pull water and minerals up through the xylem
questions.explanation: The loss of water vapour creates a pull (transpiration pull) that draws water and minerals up the xylem.

questions.q: A person whose kidneys have failed is put on dialysis. Dialysis works by:
options: Filtering wastes like urea out of the blood artificially
questions.explanation: Dialysis artificially filters nitrogenous wastes from the blood, doing the kidney's job.
